specs.name: current_time
specs.description:
Get the current date and time in a timezone. Use this whenever the answer
depends on today's date or the time of day.

timezone.description: IANA timezone name, for example America/Toronto or Asia/Kolkata.
timezone.title: Timezone

specs.name: update_plan
specs.description:
Show the user a checklist of the steps you are taking. Use it for tasks
that need three or more steps: call it before starting with the whole plan,
then again with the full updated list whenever a step's status changes.
Keep at most one step in_progress. Skip it for simple questions.

specs.name: web_search
specs.description:
Search the web. Returns titles, URLs and short snippets. Snippets are often
incomplete: use web_fetch on the most relevant URLs before relying on them.

topic.description: Use news for recent events and announcements.
topic.title: Topic

time_range.description: Only return pages published within this period.
time_range.title: Time Range

specs.name: web_fetch
specs.description:
Read a web page and return its main text as Markdown, with links. Use it
to read pages found with web_search or given by the user.

url.description: The full http(s) URL of the page to read.
url.title: Url

specs.name: record_observation
specs.description:
Record what a scheduled watch observed. Only use this when a scheduled
watch run asks you to. Call it once, with found=false if the target or value
could not be found.

input_schema.description: What a watch run saw. ``value`` is set when the extract is a number.
input_schema.title: Observation

specs.name: schedule_create
specs.description:
Propose a scheduled task or watch for the user to confirm.

Use kind=task with a prompt for recurring or one-time work ("every weekday at
8am summarize ..."), and kind=watch with a watch spec to monitor a value and
alert on a condition ("tell me when the fare drops under $1500"). Resolve
relative times ("tomorrow 8am") with current_time first, and give one-shot
times as ISO 8601 with an offset. The job stays inactive until the user
confirms it in the UI; tell the user what you proposed and the next run times
this tool returns.

Changed.description: The value moved by at least ``min_delta`` since the previous observation.
Changed.title: Changed

CronSchedule.description: Standard five-field cron, evaluated in local wall-clock time of ``timezone``.
CronSchedule.title: CronSchedule

IntervalSchedule.description: Every N seconds of elapsed time (daylight saving does not affect it).
IntervalSchedule.title: IntervalSchedule

WatchSpec.description: What to look at, what to extract, and when to raise an alert.

target.description: A URL, or a search query, describing where to look.
target.title: Target

extract.description: What to read from the target, e.g. 'lowest round-trip fare in CAD'.
extract.title: Extract

WatchSpec.title: WatchSpec

input_schema.description: The editable part of a job.

prompt.description: For tasks: what the agent should do.
prompt.title: Prompt

input_schema.title: JobSpec

specs.name: schedule_list
specs.description: List the user's scheduled tasks and watches with their status and next run.

specs.name: schedule_set_status
specs.description: Pause, resume or delete a scheduled job by id (see schedule_list).

status.description: active resumes a paused job; it cannot activate an unconfirmed one.
status.title: Status

specs.name: notify_me
specs.description:
Send the user a message by email and browser push, for example a summary
they asked to receive. It only reaches the user themselves and needs their
approval each time.

# ‘Biggest mistake homeowners can make’: What the recent BoC rate hike into a stalling economy means for your money
URL: https://ca.finance.yahoo.com/news/biggest-mistake-homeowners-recent-boc-110000184.html

‘Biggest mistake homeowners can make’: What the recent BoC rate hike into a stalling economy means for your money

Romana King

6 min read

Most Canadians learned the rule years ago: the Bank of Canada (BoC) raises interest rates when the economy is running hot. Last week's move flips that script.

On Oct. 28, the central bank lifted its key rate for the first time in more than three years. Two days later, Statistics Canada, the national statistics agency, reported the economy hadn't grown at all in August — the second flat month in a row.

Pricier borrowing, stalled growth and gas-fuelled inflation land hardest on households with variable-rate debt or an upcoming mortgage renewal. It can also quietly reward savers. Here's how the pieces fit together, and what to do before the next rate decision on Dec. 9.

Don't Miss

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

Why did the Bank of Canada raise rates if the economy is stalling?

The bank is trying to get ahead of inflation rather than respond to growth. The BoC raised its policy rate by 0.25 points to 2.5% and warned that more increases could follow. It expects inflation to climb to about 3.5% by the end of the year, above its 1% to 3% target range.

Energy is the culprit. Gas prices were up 27.8% year over year in September, according to Statistics Canada data, pushing the consumer price index (CPI) to 3.1%. Excluding gasoline, inflation was just 2.2%.

Governor Tiff Macklem said the hike aims to stop high energy costs from spilling over into "generalised inflation."

But the economy isn't cooperating. Real gross domestic product (GDP) was essentially unchanged in August, missing the 0.2% gain economists expected. Early figures point to a 0.1% dip in September, leaving third-quarter growth tracking at 1.3% annualized — below the BoC's 2% call.

Canada's big banks, including RBC, TD and National Bank, raised their prime rates to 4.70% from 4.45%, effective Oct. 29. Prime drives the rate on variable-rate mortgages, home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and most personal lines of credit.

As a rough illustration, every $100,000 of prime-linked debt now costs about $250 more in interest per year. On a $50,000 HELOC, that's roughly $125.

Adjustable-payment variable mortgages rise right away. Fixed-payment variable mortgages keep the same payment but send more of it to interest, slowing your principal paydown.

Fixed mortgage rates track bond yields rather than prime — and the BoC notes those yields have risen since July.

"I think the biggest mistake homeowners can make right now is assuming that because their monthly mortgage payment hasn't changed, their financial position hasn't changed either," explains Shael Weinreb, CEO and founder of The Home Equity Partners, a Canadian financial company based in Toronto that offers a debt-free alternative to traditional loans and reverse mortgages.

Will rates go up again in December?

Many Canadians are wondering: could rates go up again in December? Possibly. As of Oct. 30, financial markets put the odds of another hike on Dec. 9 at 57%, according to LSEG Data & Analytics.

But the survey shows that economists are split. Grantham argues the weak GDP data supports a December pause. Tu Nguyen, chief economist at RSM Canada, sees a December or January hike as roughly a toss-up, but leans towards a sooner repeat rate hike. Marc Ercolao, an economist at TD Economics, is not as convinced, stating that weaker underlying growth "could complicate the case for further tightening."

Still, the underlying message for Canadians with debt is that we should expect another quarter-point rate increase, not a return to 2023-era rates.

Is there an upside for savers?

There is an upside to these rate increases: savers win, to a degree.

Higher rates tend to lift yields on high-interest savings accounts (HISAs) and guaranteed investment certificates (GICs), which helps retirees and anyone holding cash in a tax-free savings account (TFSA).

But with CPI at 3.1% and the BoC forecasting an average of 3% in 2027, a savings account paying 2% still loses purchasing power. So, the real test is whether your after-tax return beats inflation — and for many savers this means turning liquid savings into investment earnings.

What to do now

What should Canadians do as we approach the end of 2026? It depends on your situation.

All Canadians, particularly those close to or in retirement:

Keep three to six months of expenses in an emergency fund, especially if you work in a tariff-exposed sector — wholesale trade fell 1.4% in August and auto manufacturing dropped 5.8%

Compare HISA and GIC rates, and consider a GIC ladder so some money matures every year

If you hold debt:

Direct extra cash to prime-linked debt first, starting with unsecured lines of credit, which usually carry the highest variable rates

Homeowners and property investors:

Check whether your variable mortgage payment is adjustable or fixed, and ask your lender how close you are to your trigger rate

If you renew in the next 12 to 18 months, start comparing offers early and ask about rate holds

Avoid locking into a long fixed term out of fear alone; the BoC expects inflation to return close to 2% by mid-2028

As Weinreb explains: "The objective shouldn't be to win a bet against the Bank of Canada. It should be to choose a mortgage that allows you to sleep comfortably at night, regardless of what the Bank does next."

To do this, consider the bigger picture: The BoC is choosing to risk slower growth rather than let gas prices seep into the cost of everything else. As a result, if gas prices continue to remain elevated and there's no change with the U.S. policy towards Iran, then prepare your finances for additional rate increases.

# ‘Time for the BoC to go back to the drawing board’: How economists and market bets for rate hikes are reacting to Monday’s inflation data
URL: https://www.theglobeandmail.com/investing/markets/inside-the-market/article-how-todays-inflation-data-has-moved-markets-and-bets-for-future-boc/

Listen to this article

[Learn more](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/audio/) about audio

The Canadian dollar and bond yields declined in the wake of a modestly softer-than-expected [inflation report](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/investing/markets/inside-the-market/article-how-todays-inflation-data-has-moved-markets-and-bets-for-future-boc/) this morning even as bets for a Bank of Canada rate hike this December held relatively steady.

The Canadian dollar dropped about one-tenth of a U.S. cent upon the 830 am ET data release, to 69.89 cents US. Canada’s two-year bond yield, sensitive to Bank of Canada rate policy, fell about 4 basis points to 3.317%.

Traders are pricing even odds of whether the bank will hike rates again at its next policy meeting on Dec. 9, according to overnight index swaps markets via Bloomberg data. Markets are priced for an overnight rate of 2.636% upon that policy decision - very similar to where it stood last week. The current policy rate is 2.50% after the bank hiked rates by 25 basis points on Oct. 28.

Markets are fully pricing in a quarter point rate hike by the Jan. 27, 2027 Bank of Canada meeting, and three quarter-point moves by next October.

Canada’s annual inflation rate rose by 3.1% in October, data showed on Monday, the same rate as the previous month, as higher crude oil prices continued to exert pressure on the headline number.

Analysts polled by Reuters had estimated October’s annual consumer price index to grow by 3.2% from 3.1% in the prior month, and projected monthly inflation at 0.3%. On a month-on-month basis, inflation was at 0.2% last month, Statistics Canada said.

Most of the rise in annual inflation in October was led by energy-related costs with crude oil staying firm on a year-on-year basis. Excluding energy, the annual CPI rate rose 2% in October, after increasing 2.1% in September, StatsCan said.

Several economists are suggesting market-based probabilities for a rate hike next month are too aggressive in light of the benign inflation report this morning. Here’s how they are reacting:

**Stephen Brown, chief North America economist, Capital Economics**

“There is still little evidence of indirect effects on core inflation from the surge in energy prices, suggesting that the Bank of Canada will be content to keep interest rates on hold at its last meeting of the year and will not need to hike by as much as markets are pricing in.”

“The 0.2% m/m seasonally adjusted rise in the overall CPI was half the pace we anticipated, largely thanks to a muted 0.1% gain in the CPI excluding food and energy. As a result, headline inflation was unchanged at 3.1%. There were firmer gains in some of the major categories, with clothing & footwear and health & personal care prices each rising by 0.4%. Similarly, the 0.3% increase in shelter prices was a firmer than the average so far this year. But those gains were offset by weakness elsewhere, with the recreation, education & reading, household operations, furnishings & equipment, and alcoholic beverages categories all recording price gains of just 0.1%.”

“The monthly changes in CPI-trim and CPI-median were slightly stronger than for the other core measures, rising at an average of 0.20% m/m. Nonetheless, that was the smallest average gain in four months and only marginally above the target-consistent pace of 0.17%, with the average three-month annualised rate easing to 2.7% and the average annual rate likewise edging down to 1.9%. Those figures suggest that the Bank will continue to view policy tightening through the lens of “insurance hikes” rather than the need to meaningfully tighten financial conditions. Accordingly, we remain happy with our forecast that the Bank will pause at its final meeting of the year before resuming hikes in the new year."

**Andrew Grantham, senior economist with CIBC**

“While headline inflation remains above the upper end of the Bank of Canada’s 1-3% target band, it is actually well below the Monetary Policy Report forecast of 3.4% for Q4 as a whole, and will likely ease further beneath that mark in November given the recent move in gasoline prices. There is little sign here that inflation is spreading as much and/or as quickly as the Bank of Canada seemed to fear when they raised interest rates in October, which supports or call for a hold at the December meeting.”

**Leslie Preston, managing director and senior economist, TD**

“The Bank of Canada raised interest rates in October to get ahead of an expected uptick in inflation in Canada, but the signs of hotter price gains were fairly lukewarm in October. We agree that core inflation measures are likely to head higher in the months ahead. The question is will they be hot enough to require consecutive rate hikes from the Bank of Canada as financial markets currently expect?...”

“Our estimates suggest core inflation will rise to the 2.5-3% range in the coming months, which, given the soft macro backdrop, we don’t think should warrant further tightening this year; what matters is whether the BoC agrees. We will hear from BoC Deputy Governor Toni Gravelle on Wednesday, and we will be listening for how he characterizes inflation pressures now and how confident the Bank is that inflation will heat up on a sustained basis over the coming months. Particularly given oil and gasoline prices have headed lower.”

**Benjamin Reitzes, managing director, Canadian rates and macro strategist, BMO Capital Markets**

“There’s nothing screaming rate hike in this report. However, the Bank of Canada has been focused on headline inflation and 3.1% is still a long way from the 2% target. That being said, gasoline prices are on pace to fall nearly 10% in November which on its own would bring inflation down 0.4 ppts (though base effects will partially reverse in December unless prices keep falling). There are still a few major data points before the next policy decision, but the case for another rate hike isn’t clear cut at the moment.”

**Veronica Clark, economist with Citi**

“There are still few signs of higher energy prices being passed through to other prices, with details like clothing and furniture prices a bit stronger but food prices and rents weaker than we were expecting. BoC officials in October forecasted 3.4%YoY headline CPI in Q4, but with actual data now clearly tracking a bit below that estimate. And even with a 3.4% CPI forecast, officials dovishly chose to include guidance that they will ‘proceed carefully’ with further rate hikes. We expect rates to remain unchanged in December.”

**Daniel Hyun, senior economist, KPMG Canada**

“Another soft CPI print makes the case for patience increasingly compelling, but will it be enough to sway the Bank of Canada? Three consecutive weak jobs reports and sluggish economic activity suggest the economy could use more time to recover. Still, we maintain our call for another 25-basis-point hike in December. Energy prices, particularly diesel, remain elevated despite easing from their peaks, while the other cost pressures underpinning the Bank’s forecast for inflation to remain near 3% into 2027 – higher industrial input costs, Canadian counter-tariffs and past currency depreciation – have not materially reversed. The Bank has shifted toward getting ahead of these risks rather than waiting for them to materialize, and consecutive hikes have traditionally been part of its playbook. The governor’s upcoming speech could change our assessment, but for now we suspect the Bank will stick to its tightening course.”

**David Rosenberg, founder of Rosenberg Research**

“Canadian CPI (not seasonally adjusted) came in surprisingly light in October at +0.2% MoM (consensus was at +0.3%), in stark contrast to the U.S. It may be time for the Bank of Canada to go back to the drawing board and reframe the inflation debate around the disinflationary output gap — underscored by three consecutive months of net job loss and receding nominal wage growth — posing a very powerful antidote to the imported energy price file.”

“On a seasonally-adjusted basis, the CPI rose by less than +0.2% sequentially for the faintest pulse since June. Even better, on a MoM basis, the ex. energy core rang in at +0.1% for the second month in a row — for the first time since the spring. The CPIX, which strips out the noise from the eight most volatile items as well as indirect taxes, also posted mild back-to-back price increases of +0.1% — taking the YoY trend down to +2.0% from +2.2% in September and +2.3% in August (and +2.9% a year ago) to stand at the slowest pace since December 2024, when rate hikes were the furthest thing from the central bank’s mind.”

“In other words, the Bank of Canada is missing two chambers in its smoking gun — no evidence of a pass-through to the core, and no evidence of a response in the labor market. Justification for any further rate hikes rests totally on assumptions, not reality. That is where the policy misstep comes from, as Tiff Macklem flexes his anti-inflation credentials at a time when he really doesn’t have a leg to stand on. The data have spoken. As in, the 93% chunk of the CPI that is NOT energy is back to running fractionally below the BoC’s +2% inflation objective. The ex. energy CPI trend this time last year was running at +2.8% — when inflation was not front and center on Tiff Macklem’s mind.”

**Charles St-Arnaud, chief economist with Servus credit union**

“Our new Inflation Momentum Index, which blends both momentum and breadth, increased slightly to 0% from -2%, showing a balance between upside surprise and downside surprise in price pressures in recent months. While this suggests a slight broadening in inflationary pressure in recent months, the indicator is not yet at levels that would suggest a strong acceleration of inflation.”

“Overall, CPI continues to show that inflation remains mostly driven by higher gasoline prices. As such, there is still no strong evidence that higher energy costs in recent months are being passed on to consumers, with measures of underlying inflation and its momentum remaining within the target band.”

“It is clear that the BoC decided to hike in October in response to expected increases in broader inflationary pressures to be ‘ahead of the curve’, rather than in reaction to current conditions. It took the view that it is not a matter of whether we will see greater and broader inflationary pressures, but when we will experience them.”

“As a result, whether the BoC hike in December is likely more linked to its inflation forecast than current conditions. Nevertheless, the recent weakness in the data and the lack of broad inflationary pressures reduce the likelihood that it will hike at the next meeting.”

**David Doyle, head of economics at Macquarie Group**

“Monthly trends in core measures remain firm overall and base effects suggest YoY measures are likely to rise in the months ahead. We continue to see a steady rate hike cycle ahead, with a further 100 bps of hikes by end-27. Our base case for the next 25 bps hike remains January, although as we highlighted last month, December is also a possibility.”

**Derek Holt, vice-president and head of capital markets economics, Scotiabank**

“Probably good enough to hike in December, perhaps pending further information. That about sums up the latest inflation readings out of Canada. ... Why is it good enough? For one, the BoC is forward-looking and expects a protracted overshoot of its 2% target throughout much of its forecast horizon. That signals it believes it is behind in fighting inflationary pressures and inflation risk. That signals belief that it is not focused upon backward data to begin with and certainly not just one month.”

“Second, the smoothed core measures continue to point toward rising pressures on underlying inflation.”

**Dr. Tu Nguyen, economist for RSM Canada**

“Given both the flat core and headline inflation readings, combined with a soft job market and the drop in oil prices in November, we expect the Bank of Canada to hold its policy rate at 2.5 per cent in its December announcement.”

**CPA Canada’s chief economist David-Alexandre Brassard**

“Headline inflation remained high, but it continues to be driven largely by elevated oil prices. Core inflation actually fell to below the central bank’s two per cent target, so the data isn’t pointing to broader inflationary pressure.”

“October’s data isn’t calling for another rate hike. The Bank has already moved, and the latest numbers give it room to hold for now and see how inflation evolves.”

*With reports from Reuters*
